analogy.p: Push a shopping trolley across a smooth pavement and onto a grass verge at an angle. The wheel that reaches the grass first is slowed down, while the other wheel is still rolling quickly on the pavement, so the trolley swings round and ends up heading more directly into the grass: it has turned **towards the normal**. This is exactly what the end of a wavefront does when it enters a slower medium. If the trolley goes from grass back to pavement the first wheel speeds up and the trolley swings **away from the normal**. The analogy breaks down because a trolley is a rigid object with two wheels, whereas a wave has a continuous wavefront, and a wave's **frequency** stays constant while the wavelength changes.
analogy.t: A shopping trolley crossing from pavement to grass

bullets: Know the four outcomes at a boundary: **absorbed**, **transmitted**, **reflected** and **refracted**.
Know the **law of reflection**: **angle of incidence = angle of reflection**, both measured from the **normal**.
Know the difference between **specular** and **diffuse** reflection.
Know that **refraction** is a change of **direction** caused by a change of **speed**.
Know the rules: slower medium means bending **towards the normal**; faster medium means bending **away from the normal**; along the normal there is **no change of direction**.
Higher tier: **explain refraction using wavefronts**.
Link: wave speed, frequency and wavelength come from **v = f λ** (previous spec points).
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA 8463 expects you to know that **waves can be absorbed, transmitted, reflected or refracted at the boundary between two different materials**, and that what happens depends on the wavelength of the wave and the properties of the materials. You must be able to **construct ray diagrams** to show reflection and to show **refraction** at a boundary, and (Higher tier) to **use wavefront diagrams to explain refraction in terms of the change of speed** when a wave moves into a different medium. This is the physics behind mirrors, lenses, echoes, ultrasound scans and seismology, so it is examined as drawing, explanation and calculation questions.

bullets: **Reflected:** the wave **bounces back** into the first medium at the boundary.
**Transmitted:** the wave **passes through** into the second medium; if its direction changes, it is **refracted**.
**Absorbed:** the wave's energy is **transferred to the material** (for example, a black surface warms up in sunlight).
Usually a **mixture** occurs: a window reflects a little light, absorbs a little and transmits most.
The result depends on **the wavelength** of the wave and the **properties** of the two materials.
**Energy is conserved:** the reflected, transmitted and absorbed energy add up to the energy that arrived.
All types of wave show these behaviours: **light, sound, water waves, seismic waves** and all other electromagnetic waves.
core.h: What can happen to a wave at a boundary
core.p: A **boundary** is the surface where one material (medium) meets another, such as air and glass or air and water. When a wave arrives at a boundary, its energy can be dealt with in several ways at once. Some of the wave may be **reflected** (it bounces back into the first medium), some may be **transmitted** (it passes into the second medium), and some may be **absorbed** (the wave energy is transferred to the material, usually as internal energy so the material warms up). Which of these happens most depends on the **wavelength** of the wave and on the **materials** involved.

bullets: **Law of reflection: angle of incidence (i) = angle of reflection (r).**
The **normal** is drawn at **90° to the surface**, as a **dashed line**.
Angles are always measured **from the normal**, not from the surface of the mirror.
If a ray makes **35° with the mirror surface**, the angle of incidence is **90° − 35° = 55°**.
The angle **between the incident and reflected rays** is **i + r = 2i**.
A ray that hits **along the normal** (i = 0°) is reflected **straight back** along the same path.
Reflection **does not change the speed, wavelength or frequency** of the wave, because it stays in the same medium.
The law works for **all waves**: light in mirrors, sound in echoes and water waves bouncing off a barrier.
core.h: Reflection and the law of reflection
core.p: Reflection happens when a wave bounces off a boundary and returns into the medium it came from. Light reflecting from a mirror is the standard example. To describe reflection precisely you draw a **normal**, which is a line drawn at **90°** to the surface at the point where the ray strikes. The **incident ray** is the ray arriving, and the **reflected ray** is the ray leaving. The **angle of incidence (i)** is the angle between the incident ray and the normal, and the **angle of reflection (r)** is the angle between the reflected ray and the normal. The **law of reflection** states that **the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection**, and the incident ray, the normal and the reflected ray all lie in the same plane.

bullets: **Specular reflection:** from a **smooth** surface; reflected rays remain **parallel**; produces a **clear image**.
**Diffuse reflection:** from a **rough** surface; reflected rays are **scattered**; no clear image forms.
In **both** cases **each ray obeys the law of reflection** at the point where it strikes.
Diffuse reflection is what lets us **see non-shiny objects** from many directions.
Whether a surface is 'smooth' depends on the **wavelength**: a surface rough for light can be smooth for radio waves, so a mesh dish can reflect **microwaves** and **radio waves**.

**Plane mirror image:** it appears the **same distance behind** the mirror as the object is in front, is the **same size** and is **laterally inverted** (not named in the AQA spec but often used in questions).
A **rough road** that is wet becomes smoother because water fills the gaps, giving more **specular** reflection (glare).
core.p: Whether a surface gives a clear mirror image depends on how smooth it is compared with the wavelength of the wave. A **smooth, flat surface** such as a mirror causes **specular reflection**: parallel rays arriving at the surface are all reflected in the same direction, so they stay parallel and form a clear image. A **rough surface** such as paper, cloth or a wall causes **diffuse reflection**: the surface has many tiny faces pointing in different directions, so each ray follows the law of reflection but the normals point in different directions, and the reflected rays are **scattered** in all directions. This is why you can see a wall from any position in the room, but only see your face from certain angles in a mirror.

bullets: **Transparent** materials **transmit** most of the light that reaches them (for example clear glass).
**Opaque** materials transmit **none**; the light is **reflected or absorbed**.
**Absorbed waves** transfer energy to the **internal (thermal) energy store** of the material.
**Dark, matt surfaces** are good absorbers; **light, shiny surfaces** are good reflectors.
**Ordinary glass** transmits **visible light** but absorbs much **ultraviolet**; the **atmosphere** absorbs most UV from the Sun.
**Metals** reflect radio waves and microwaves, which is why **satellite dishes** are made of metal.
**Ultrasound** is partly reflected at the boundaries between different body tissues, which is used to build up scan images.
core.p: The specification states that different substances may **absorb, transmit, refract or reflect** electromagnetic waves in ways that **vary with wavelength**. A **transparent** material such as clear glass **transmits** most visible light, passing it through with little absorption. An **opaque** material such as a brick wall does not allow light through, and instead reflects or absorbs it. Absorbed energy is **transferred to the internal energy store** of the material, which is why dark surfaces get warm in the Sun. The same material can behave differently for different wavelengths: ordinary glass transmits visible light but absorbs much of the ultraviolet.

bullets: **Refraction = change of direction caused by change of speed** (when a wave crosses a boundary at an angle).
Light is **slower in glass or water** than in air.
**Entering a slower medium:** the ray bends **towards the normal** (the angle gets smaller).
**Entering a faster medium:** the ray bends **away from the normal** (the angle gets bigger).
**Along the normal (0°):** the wave **slows down or speeds up** but is **not bent**.
The greater the **change in speed**, the **greater the bending**; this is linked to how **optically dense** the material is.
Not every wave is refracted: if the wave **hits at 90° to the boundary** there is no change of direction.
Refraction happens because the **speed changes**, not because the material is 'denser' in itself; always give the speed in your explanation.
core.h: Refraction: what it is and why it happens
core.p: **Refraction** is the **change in direction** of a wave as it passes from one medium into another, caused by a **change in the speed** of the wave. Waves travel at different speeds in different substances. For light, the speed is greatest in a vacuum (about **3.0 × 10⁸ m/s**), slightly less in air, and noticeably less in water (about 2.25 × 10⁸ m/s) and glass (about 2.0 × 10⁸ m/s). If a wave hits the boundary at an **angle** and changes speed, its direction changes. If it hits the boundary **along the normal** (at 90°), the speed still changes but the direction **does not**.

bullets: **Air → glass** (slows): bends **towards the normal**; angle in glass **smaller** than in air.
**Glass → air** (speeds up): bends **away from the normal**; angle in air **larger** than in glass.
**Air → water** (slows): bends **towards** the normal; **water → air**: bends **away**.
The **normal does not change**: it is always drawn at **90° to the boundary** at the point of entry.
The **angle of refraction (r)** is measured **between the refracted ray and the normal**.
If a ray **leaves a parallel-sided block** it returns to the **original direction**, so the **emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray**.
The ray is **shifted sideways** (lateral displacement) but not turned overall.
A thicker block or a bigger angle of incidence gives a **bigger sideways shift**.
core.h: Optical density and the direction of bending
core.p: Examiners often use the term **optical density**: a material that is more **optically dense** slows light down more. Glass is more optically dense than air, and water is more optically dense than air. A ray going from a **less dense to a more dense** medium (for example air to glass) **slows down** and bends **towards the normal**, while a ray going from **more dense to less dense** (glass to air) **speeds up** and bends **away from the normal**. A helpful memory is that the ray **bends towards the normal when it slows** and **away when it speeds up**. When asked to draw refraction, the direction of the bend is the main mark, so check it every time.

bullets: **Frequency:** **unchanged** (set by the source).
**Speed:** **changes** (slower in the denser medium).
**Wavelength:** **changes** with the speed: **shorter** when slower, **longer** when faster.
**Direction:** changes if the wave meets the boundary at an **angle** other than 90°.
**Amplitude:** usually **decreases** because some energy is reflected or absorbed.
Because **v = f λ** and f is constant, **v and λ are directly proportional**: if the speed halves, so does the wavelength.
Example: red light of frequency 4.5 × 10¹⁴ Hz has λ = 6.7 × 10⁻⁷ m in air and about **4.4 × 10⁻⁷ m** in glass where it travels at 2.0 × 10⁸ m/s.
The **colour** of light is decided by its **frequency**, so light does not change colour when it enters glass.
core.h: What changes and what stays the same in refraction
core.p: This is a very common exam question. When a wave is refracted, its **frequency stays the same**, because the frequency is set by the source and the same number of waves arrive at the boundary each second as leave it. The **speed changes**, and because **v = f λ** with f constant, the **wavelength changes in the same proportion** as the speed. If the wave slows down, the wavelength gets **shorter**; if it speeds up, the wavelength gets **longer**. The **direction** changes only if the wave meets the boundary at an angle.

bullets: Draw the **boundary** first, then the **normal** (dashed, at 90°) at the point where the ray meets it.
Draw the **incident ray** to the point on the boundary; **add an arrow** pointing towards the boundary.
For **reflection**, draw the **reflected ray** with the same angle to the normal on the opposite side.
For **refraction into glass**, draw the ray inside the block **closer to the normal** than the incident ray.
At the **second surface**, draw a new normal and bend the ray **away from it**, so the **emergent ray is parallel** to the original incident ray.
Label **i** (between incident ray and normal) and **r** or **e** between the other ray and normal, **not between the ray and the surface**.
Use **straight lines** only, with a ruler, and make the rays meet exactly **at the boundary**.
In a drawing, a **small angle of incidence** gives **little bending**; a ray along the normal is **not bent** at all.
core.h: Drawing ray diagrams for refraction and reflection
core.p: Ray diagram marks are for accuracy and for following the conventions, so learn them. Use a **sharp pencil and a ruler**, draw the **normal as a dashed line** at 90° to the surface, put **arrows** on the rays to show direction, and label the **angle of incidence (i)** and **angle of refraction (r)** or reflection. Use a **protractor** if angles are given, and make sure the bend is in the correct direction.

bullets: A **wavefront** is drawn **perpendicular to the direction of travel**, and the **ray** is drawn at 90° to the wavefronts.
The part of the wavefront **entering the slower medium first slows down**.
The rest of the wavefront is **still moving faster**, so it covers a **greater distance** in the same time.
This makes the wavefront **change angle** (pivot), so the **direction of the wave changes**.
In the slower medium the **wavelength is shorter**, so the **wavefronts are closer together**.
**Frequency stays the same**, so the same number of wavefronts cross the boundary each second.
If the wave **speeds up** (for example glass to air), the pattern is reversed: wavefronts spread out and the ray bends **away from the normal**.
If the wavefront is **parallel to the boundary** (hits at 90°), **all** of it changes speed together, so there is **no change of direction**.
core.p: At Higher tier you must **explain refraction in terms of the change of speed**, usually using **wavefronts**. A wavefront is a line joining points of a wave that are in step, for example all the crests, and it is drawn at **right angles to the direction of travel**. Imagine a wavefront hitting a boundary at an angle. The **end of the wavefront that reaches the slower medium first slows down**, while the other end is still travelling at the faster speed. In the same time the faster end travels further, so the wavefront **pivots** and the direction of travel **turns towards the normal**. In the slower medium the wavefronts are **closer together** because the wavelength is shorter, but they arrive at the boundary at the same rate, so the **frequency is unchanged**.

bullets: **Shallow region (slower):** wavelength **shorter**, wavefronts **closer together**, direction **bends towards the normal**.
**Deep region (faster):** wavelength **longer**, wavefronts **further apart**.
**Frequency does not change**, because the dipper sets it.
If the waves hit the shallow region **head on**, they slow down but **do not change direction**.
A strobe light is used to make the pattern **appear to stand still** so wavelength can be measured.
You can **measure the wavelength** in each region and show that **v = f λ** gives a smaller speed in the shallow region.
This shows that **refraction is caused by a change of speed**, and that the effect is the same for **any type of wave**.
core.h: Refraction of water waves in a ripple tank
core.p: Water waves provide a clear way to see refraction, because the speed of ripples depends on the **depth** of the water. In **shallow water** the waves travel **more slowly** than in deeper water. If a flat piece of plastic or glass is placed on the bottom of a ripple tank to make a **shallow region**, straight waves that meet its edge at an angle slow down, their wavelength shortens, and their direction changes towards the normal. This is the same behaviour as light entering glass, so the ripple tank is a good **model** for light, but with waves slow enough to watch.

bullets: **Pencil in water appears bent**; **pool appears shallower**: light refracts away from the normal as it leaves the water.
**Lenses** (eye, camera, glasses) use **refraction** to focus light.
**Echoes** and **sonar**: sound waves **reflect** from surfaces, and the **time delay** gives distance.
**Ultrasound scans**: partial **reflection** at boundaries between tissues.
**Seismic waves** are **reflected and refracted** at boundaries inside the Earth, giving evidence about its layers.
**Sound** can also refract when the **temperature** of the air changes, because the speed of sound depends on temperature.
**Optical fibres** use reflection to keep light inside (beyond GCSE detail).
**Mirror in a periscope or car mirror** use the **law of reflection**.
core.p: Refraction and reflection explain many familiar observations. A **pencil in a glass of water** looks bent at the surface because light from the part under water is refracted as it leaves the water, and a **swimming pool looks shallower** than it really is for the same reason. **Lenses** work by refracting light so that rays are brought together or spread apart (this is covered with ray diagrams for lenses). **Reflection** gives **echoes** from walls and cliffs, **mirror images**, **radar** and **sonar**, and the reflection of **ultrasound** at tissue boundaries is used for scans. Seismic waves are also reflected and refracted inside the Earth, which gave the evidence for the structure of the Earth's core.

bullets: **Angle of incidence = 90° − angle between ray and mirror.**
The angle **between incident and reflected rays** = **2 × angle of incidence**.
**Frequency does not change at a boundary**: find f in the first medium from f = v ÷ λ and use it in the second.
**New wavelength = new speed ÷ frequency**.
**Ratio rule:** λ₂ ÷ λ₁ = v₂ ÷ v₁ (because f is constant).
Convert **nm to m** by multiplying by **10⁻⁹**; write very large or small answers in **standard form**.
Light speed in a vacuum is **3.0 × 10⁸ m/s**; sound in air is about **340 m/s**.
Check your answer is **sensible**: the wavelength must be **shorter** in the medium where the wave is slower.
core.p: Although there is no single equation just for refraction at GCSE, you need to combine **v = f λ** with the ideas above, and to calculate **angles** correctly. For angle questions, take care to measure from the **normal**, and remember that the angle between the ray and the mirror is **90° minus** the angle of incidence. For a wave entering a new medium, the **frequency is the same on both sides**, so you can calculate the new wavelength from the new speed. Showing the equation, the substitution and the unit earns the method marks.

bullets: **Ripple tank practical:** shows refraction when water depth changes.
**Wave properties:** v = f λ is needed to explain what changes at a boundary.
**EM spectrum:** different wavelengths are absorbed, reflected, transmitted or refracted differently by different materials.
**Lenses and images:** refraction at curved surfaces focuses light.
**Sound and ultrasound:** reflection at boundaries is used in sonar, echo-location and medical scanning.
**Seismic waves:** reflection and refraction at layer boundaries give evidence for the Earth's structure.
**Energy:** absorbed waves increase the **internal energy** of a material (link to energy and heating topics).
core.p: Reflection and refraction connect much of the Waves topic. The **electromagnetic spectrum** topic uses these ideas to explain how different wavelengths behave at boundaries, for example why microwaves are reflected by metal but pass through glass. **Lenses** depend on refraction to form images, and the **ripple tank practical** gives experimental evidence. **Sound and ultrasound** use reflection for echoes and scans, and **seismic waves** use both reflection and refraction to reveal the structure of the Earth. Making these links explicit strengthens your answers to extended-response questions.

exam: **State/Name (1 mark):** give the exact term: 'normal', 'angle of incidence', 'refraction'. A definition must include the cause: 'change in direction caused by a change in speed'.
**Law of reflection (1 mark):** 'angle of incidence = angle of reflection', and say they are measured from the normal.

**Draw a ray diagram (2 to 3 marks):** dashed normal at 90°, straight ruled rays with arrows, equal angles for reflection, and the correct direction of bend for refraction (towards the normal into a slower medium).
**Explain why light bends (2 to 3 marks):** the light slows down in the glass (1) so it changes direction (1) towards the normal (1). Always mention the change in speed.

**Specular v diffuse (2 marks):** smooth surface, parallel rays stay parallel, clear image; rough surface, rays scattered in many directions, no clear image. Mention that each ray still obeys the law.
**What changes in refraction (2 to 3 marks):** speed and wavelength change; frequency stays the same; direction changes if the ray meets the boundary at an angle.

**Higher tier wavefront explanation (3 to 4 marks):** the part of the wavefront entering the slower medium first slows down; the other part is still faster so travels further; the wavefront changes direction (towards the normal); the wavelength is shorter and the frequency unchanged.
**Calculation (2 to 3 marks):** show the equation (v = f λ), keep the frequency constant across the boundary, convert units (nm to m), give the unit and use standard form where needed.
**Angle questions:** subtract from 90° when the angle is given to the mirror, and remember the angle between incident and reflected rays is double the angle of incidence.
**Absorb, transmit, reflect:** link to wavelength and the material, and say absorbed energy is transferred to the internal energy of the material.

mistakes.r: The angle of incidence is measured between the ray and the normal (the line at 90° to the mirror).
mistakes.w: The angle of incidence is the angle between the ray and the mirror.

mistakes.r: The normal is drawn at 90° to the surface as a dashed line, at the point where the ray strikes.
mistakes.w: The normal is drawn along the surface, or as a solid line.

mistakes.r: Light slows down in glass, so it bends towards the normal; refraction is caused by the change of speed.
mistakes.w: Light bends towards the normal because glass is denser.

mistakes.r: The frequency stays the same; the speed and wavelength change.
mistakes.w: The wavelength and frequency both change when light enters glass.

mistakes.r: If the ray meets the boundary along the normal (at 90°) its speed changes but its direction does not.
mistakes.w: Light always bends when it crosses a boundary.

mistakes.r: Leaving glass into air the ray speeds up and bends away from the normal.
mistakes.w: Light leaving glass bends towards the normal.

mistakes.r: Each ray still obeys the law of reflection; the surface is rough so the normals point in different directions.
mistakes.w: Diffuse reflection does not obey the law of reflection.

mistakes.r: Absorbed wave energy is transferred to the material, increasing its internal energy so it warms up.
At the second surface the ray bends away from the normal, so the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray.
mistakes.w: The emergent ray from a glass block is bent towards the normal again.

mistakes.r: Use a ruler, straight lines and arrows showing the direction of travel.
mistakes.w: Rays drawn without arrows or with a freehand curve.

summary: AQA 8463: you must know that waves can be absorbed, transmitted, reflected or refracted at a boundary, apply the law of reflection (angle of incidence = angle of reflection, measured from the normal), explain specular and diffuse reflection, draw ray diagrams for refraction, and (Higher tier) explain refraction using wavefronts as a change in wave speed. It underpins mirrors, lenses, echoes, ultrasound and seismic waves.

terms.d: The surface where two different media meet, for example air and glass.
A material through which a wave travels.
A line drawn at 90° to a surface at the point where a ray meets it; angles are measured from the normal.
The ray of light (or wave direction) arriving at a boundary.
The ray that bounces back from a boundary into the first medium.
The angle between the incident ray and the normal.
The angle between the reflected ray and the normal.
The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
Reflection from a smooth surface in which parallel rays stay parallel, giving a clear image.
Reflection from a rough surface in which rays are scattered in many directions.
When a wave transfers its energy to a material, increasing its internal energy.
When a wave passes through a material and continues on the other side.
The change in direction of a wave as it passes from one medium to another, caused by a change in the speed of the wave.
The angle between the refracted ray and the normal.
A measure of how much a material slows light down; light travels more slowly in a more optically dense material.
The ray that leaves a block or lens after refraction.
A line joining points of a wave that are in step, drawn at right angles to the direction of travel.
The number of waves passing a point per second; it does not change when a wave is refracted.
Allows light to pass through with little absorption, so objects can be seen clearly through it.
Does not allow light to pass through; the light is absorbed or reflected.

worked.q: A ray of light strikes a plane mirror so that it makes an angle of 35° with the surface of the mirror. (a) Calculate the angle of incidence. (b) State the angle of reflection. (c) Calculate the angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray. (3 marks)
steps: The normal is at 90° to the mirror surface, so the angle of incidence = 90° − 35° = 55°.
Law of reflection: angle of reflection = angle of incidence = 55°.
Angle between incident and reflected rays = 55° + 55° = 110°.

worked.ans: (a) 6.7 × 10⁻⁷ m in air and 4.4 × 10⁻⁷ m in glass (ratio 2:3, the same as the speeds); (b) 4.5 × 10¹⁴ Hz; (c) it bends towards the normal.
worked.q: Red light of frequency 4.5 × 10¹⁴ Hz travels at 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s in air and 2.0 × 10⁸ m/s in glass. (a) Calculate the wavelength in air and in glass. (b) State the frequency of the light in glass. (c) State how a ray entering the glass at an angle is affected. (4 marks)
steps: The frequency does not change at a boundary, so it is still 4.5 × 10¹⁴ Hz.
The light slows down in glass, so the ray bends towards the normal.

worked.ans: Model answer: Each wavefront meets the boundary at an angle, so one end enters the slower medium first and slows down. The other end is still moving at the faster speed and so covers a greater distance in the same time. The wavefront therefore changes direction and the wave bends towards the normal. In the slower medium the wavelength is shorter and the wavefronts are closer together, but the frequency stays the same.
worked.q: Use wavefronts to explain why a wave bends towards the normal when it enters a slower medium at an angle. (4 marks, Higher tier)
steps: Wavefronts are at right angles to the direction of travel.
The end of the wavefront that meets the boundary first enters the slower medium and slows down.
The other end is still travelling at the faster speed, so in the same time it travels further.
This makes the wavefront turn (pivot), so the direction of travel changes towards the normal; the wavelength is shorter but the frequency is unchanged.
